In [[geometry]], the '''Gram–Euler theorem''',<ref name=":0" /> '''Gram-Sommerville, Brianchon-Gram''' or '''Gram relation'''<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Camenga|first=Kristin A.|date=2006|title=Angle sums on polytopes and polytopal complexes|journal=Cornell University|arxiv=math/0607469 }}</ref> (named after [[Jørgen Pedersen Gram]], [[Leonhard Euler]], [[Duncan Sommerville]] and [[Charles Julien Brianchon]]) is a generalization of the [[Internal and external angles#Properties|internal angle sum formula]] of [[polygon|polygons]] to higher-dimensional [[Polytope|polytopes]]. The equation constrains the sums of the interior angles of a polytope in a manner analogous to the [[Euler characteristic|Euler relation]] on the number of d-dimensional [[Face (geometry)|faces]]. 

== Statement ==
Let <math>P</math> be an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Convex set|convex]] [[polytope]]. For each ''k''-[[Face (geometry)|face]] <math>F</math>, with <math>k = \dim(F)</math> its dimension (0 for vertices, 1 for edges, 2 for faces, etc., up to ''n'' for ''P'' itself), its [[Internal and external angles|interior]] (higher-dimensional) [[solid angle]] <math>\angle(F)</math> is defined by choosing a small enough <math>(n - 1)</math>-[[sphere]] centered at some point in the interior of <math>F</math> and finding the surface area contained inside <math>P</math>. Then the Gram–Euler theorem states:<ref>{{Cite book|last=Grünbaum|first=Branko|title=Convex Polytopes|title-link=Convex Polytopes|date=October 2003|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-387-40409-7|location=|pages=297–303}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Perles|first1=M. A.|last2=Shepard|first2=G. C.|date=1967|title=Angle sums of convex polytopes|journal=Mathematica Scandinavica|volume=21|issue=2|pages=199–218|doi=10.7146/math.scand.a-10860|jstor=24489707|issn=0025-5521|doi-access=free}}</ref> <math display="block">\sum_{F \subset P} (-1)^{\dim F} \angle(F) = 0</math>In [[non-Euclidean geometry]] of constant curvature (i.e. [[Spherical geometry|spherical]], <math>\epsilon = 1</math>, and [[Hyperbolic geometry|hyperbolic]], <math>\epsilon = -1</math>, geometry) the relation gains a volume term, but only if the dimension ''n'' is even:<math display="block">\sum_{F \subset P} (-1)^{\dim F} \angle(F) = \epsilon^{n/2}(1 + (-1)^n)\operatorname{Vol}(P)</math>Here, <math>\operatorname{Vol}(P)</math> is the normalized (hyper)volume of the polytope (i.e, the fraction of the ''n''-dimensional spherical or hyperbolic space); the angles <math>\angle(F)</math> also have to be expressed as fractions (of the (''n''-1)-sphere).<ref name=":1" />

When the polytope is [[Simplicial polytope|simplicial]] additional angle restrictions known as ''Perles relations'' hold, analogous to the [[Dehn-Sommerville equations]] for the number of faces.<ref name=":1" />

== Examples ==

For a two-dimensional polygon, the statement expands into:<math display="block">\sum_{v} \alpha_v - \sum_e \pi + 2\pi = 0</math>where the first term <math>A=\textstyle\sum \alpha_v</math> is the sum of the internal vertex angles, the second sum is over the edges, each of which has internal angle <math>\pi</math>, and the final term corresponds to the entire polygon, which has a full internal angle <math>2\pi</math>. For a polygon with <math>n</math> faces, the theorem tells us that <math>A - \pi n + 2\pi = 0</math>, or equivalently, <math>A = \pi (n - 2)</math>. For a polygon on a sphere, the relation gives the spherical surface area or [[solid angle]] as the [[spherical excess]]: <math>\Omega = A - \pi (n - 2)</math>.

For a three-dimensional [[polyhedron]] the theorem reads:<math display="block">\sum_{v} \Omega_v - 2\sum_e \theta_e + \sum_f 2\pi - 4\pi = 0</math>where <math>\Omega_v</math> is the solid angle at a vertex, <math>\theta_e</math> the [[dihedral angle]] at an edge (the solid angle of the corresponding [[Spherical lune|lune]] is twice as big), the third sum counts the faces (each with an interior hemisphere angle of <math>2\pi</math>) and the last term is the interior solid angle (full sphere or <math>4\pi</math>). 

== History ==
The n-dimensional relation was first proven by [[Duncan Sommerville|Sommerville]], Heckman and [[Branko Grünbaum|Grünbaum]] for the spherical, hyperbolic and Euclidean case, respectively.<ref name=":1" />
